title: The Language of Room 214
premise: Mireille Delacroix, a failed translator drifting through a loveless marriage to bridge inspector Theo, is recruited by Odile Vasseur, the last fluent speaker of a dying immigrant tongue, to learn it before Odile dies. As Mireille's lessons deepen, she discovers Odile's language holds the key to a family secret: the question Theo's family arranged itself around decades ago — what happened the night Odile's brother disappeared and Theo's father drove the last bus out of the old neighborhood. Learning the words means learning the truth, and the truth will either dissolve her marriage or finally give her a self to stand inside. In the end, Mireille becomes the language's second-to-last speaker, speaks the question aloud at Odile's deathbed, and chooses to leave the marriage — carrying the language, and herself, out of Room 214.
about_author: L. M. Yarrow is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent fifteen years listening to testimony in languages she was never allowed to answer in. She writes about translation, silence, and the small betrayals that hold families together.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He inspects a failing bridge, measuring cracks in millimeters, and comes home to measure the same cracks in his marriage. Mireille has stopped finishing sentences. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as competence.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. She moves through her own house like a renter, cataloguing what she'd take if she left. A flyer for a 'dying languages' archive catches her eye at the library. Beat: restlessness with no destination.

chapters.title: Room 214
chapters.summary: Mireille answers the archive ad and meets Odile Vasseur, ninety-one, in a community college classroom that smells of chalk and camphor. Odile tests her with a word that has no English equivalent. Beat: the first spark of being seen.

chapters.title: A Word for What the River Carries
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. First real lesson. Odile teaches words for things the old neighborhood lost: the bakery, the flood, the name of the street before it was renamed. Beat: grief arriving disguised as vocabulary.

chapters.title: Theo Measures the Span
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He notices Mireille humming in a language he half-recognizes from childhood — his grandmother's kitchen. He says nothing. Beat: recognition and cowardice in the same breath.

chapters.title: Homework
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. She practices aloud in the shower, at red lights, over dinner. Theo asks what language it is; she lies for the first time in years. Beat: the thrill and guilt of a secret self.

chapters.title: The Last Bus Route
chapters.summary: Odile's POV (first of three). Memory chapter: 1968, the night the city rerouted the bus line that connected the immigrant neighborhood to the rest of the town, and her brother Léo didn't come home. Beat: the wound the whole book orbits.

chapters.title: Conjugating the Past
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. Odile begins refusing certain words, certain nights. Mireille realizes the lessons have holes shaped like a person. Beat: suspicion blooming into obligation.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing Walls
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. His sister calls: their father's nursing home wants to move him, and someone must sort the boxes in the garage. He defers, again. Beat: a family built to never ask questions.

chapters.title: The Garage
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. Sorting Theo's father's boxes, she finds a bus driver's cap and a photograph of Odile's brother. She pockets the photo. Beat: the secret becomes hers to hold.

chapters.title: Irregular Verbs
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She recognizes Mireille's surname and says nothing, testing instead whether the girl will ask the question herself. Beat: the teacher's terrible patience.

chapters.title: What the Family Arranged Itself Around
chapters.summary: Mireille confronts Theo with the photograph. He shuts down completely — the marriage's load-bearing silence, finally visible. Beat: open rupture.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Odile finally names it in her language, then in English: 'Did your father-in-law leave my brother on the bridge, or take him with him?' Mireille realizes she is holding both families' survival. Beat: the book's central question made explicit.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He digs into his father's nursing-home lucid hours, drives to the old neighborhood, walks the decommissioned bridge he once inspected. Beat: a man learning to look at what he's avoided.

chapters.title: Two Speakers
chapters.summary: Mireille and Odile translate the nursing-home records together, word by word. Odile's health fails mid-session; she makes Mireille promise to finish the sentence even if she can't. Beat: transmission becomes urgent.

chapters.title: The Father's Answer
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. His father, briefly lucid, gives a partial answer: he took Léo on the bus that night, and Léo got off at the bridge — by choice, to start a new life, or to end one. The records end there. Beat: truth arriving incomplete, which is worse.

chapters.title: Expansion
chapters.summary: Mireille and Theo fight with everything they've never said — the marriage, the baby they didn't have, the tenant arrangement of their lives. Beat: climax of the marriage; both finally owners of their anger.

chapters.title: The Bridge at Night
chapters.summary: Mireille walks the old bridge alone, speaking Odile's language aloud to the river, and understands Léo's choice as her own mirror: stay and vanish, or leave and live. Beat: internal climax.

chapters.title: Deathbed Grammar
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. On her last night, Mireille asks the question aloud, formally, in the language. Odile answers: 'The bus left. That is all a language can say.' Beat: the question answered by refusing a definitive answer — and it is enough.

chapters.title: The Archive
chapters.summary: Mireille records the final lessons; Odile dies with Mireille's hand in hers, the last word spoken to another speaker. Beat: succession, grief, and the strange honor of outliving your teacher.

chapters.title: Second-to-Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. At the funeral, Theo reaches for her hand; she lets him hold it, then lets go. She signs the lease on her own apartment and enrolls to teach the language to three new students. Beat: the price of survival paid, and worth it.

chapters.title: Room 215
chapters.summary: Final chapter, alternating brief POVs. Mireille teaches her first class in a different room, with a new sign on the door. Theo, on his bridge, says a word of the language to the river. Beat: quiet resolution — the language survives by changing hands, and so does she.
